description: We will be working on building a junior astronaut mission trainer.
summary:
Outpost Zero is a top-down 2D game in the style of Stardew Valley, made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players run a lunar or Martian outpost and balance power, air, radiation shielding and food. It’s aimed at kids 7–12, parents and space fans, and runs in any browser (plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no install).

The challenge: space STEM content is either too simple, so real trade-offs vanish, or too complex for young learners. Outpost Zero makes them tangible: turning on one machine drains the battery something else needs.

How it plays

Dr. Nova, a scientist on Earth, gives missions and explains each problem the first time it happens.
Your robot buddy Bolt helps run the base. Missions earn rover parts; in Judge demo mode the rover starts built and fast travel is open.
Real NASA data: solar flares from NASA’s DONKI service drive shield and radiation decisions. If the live feed fails, flares are clearly labelled archived or typical.
Two worlds: the Moon, and Mars with a weaker sun, dust storms, slow radio and a robot explorer. Mars includes a frosty Southern Highlands and the Viking 1 site in the Northern Lowlands.
Real NASA photos and clips, including Curiosity sulfur crystals, Viking 1’s first photos, Ingenuity and the Apollo hammer-and-feather drop.
Keyboard navigation, a daily-missions list and highlight hands pointing at HUD bars.
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Outpost Zero is a top-down 2D game, in the style of Stardew Valley. The player runs a Moon or Mars outpost and keeps four systems balanced: power, air, radiation shielding and food. Every choice has a cost. Turning on the lab or greenhouse drains the battery that the air generator or shield also needs. Dr. Nova, a friendly scientist on Earth, gives missions and explains each problem the first time it happens. The player also walks the base, mines ice, grows food, studies samples and sends research to Earth for rover parts. Solar flares arrive on a schedule and the player must raise the shield in time. The flares come from NASA’s DONKI service. If the live feed is unavailable, the game uses archived flares and labels them as archived. Mars changes the rules with a weaker sun, dust storms, slow radio and a robot explorer instead of a person.

What benefits does it have?

Tangible trade-offs: students feel why missions succeed or fail instead of reading about it.

Fail safely: a blackout teaches more than a paragraph does.

Real facts: pop-ups use real NASA photos and clips, such as Curiosity’s sulfur crystals, Viking 1’s first photos from Mars, Ingenuity’s flight, and the Apollo hammer-and-feather drop.

Free and easy to use: it runs in any browser with no install. It supports keyboard play and has a Judge demo mode for a quick tour.

What is the intended impact?

The aim is to make engineering trade-offs interesting to ages 7–12, and to leave students curious about the real missions behind each pop-up. It could be used in classrooms, at home, or by space fans.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did you use?

Languages: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, drawn on an HTML canvas, with no build step or game engine.

Data: NASA DONKI (solar flares) and the NASA Image and Video Library, plus bundled photos from NASA missions.

AI: Claude wrote the code, and it also drafted the presentation and script. The team directed it and tested the game in a browser.

Testing: 46 automated checks for the game rules in Node.js, and browser tests with Playwright and headless Chrome.

Sharing: GitHub and Google Drive.

Hardware: no special hardware. It runs on an ordinary laptop or desktop.

How is it creative?

It turns outpost engineering into a charming pixel-art world. The characters include Dr. Nova, the robot buddy Bolt, and the alien Zorp. Sound, animation and real photos support the story: a Moon base with real flares, a Mars base with dust storms, and the Viking 1 landing site. Each world follows its own rules, rather than being a re-skin of the other.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty: the game never pretends archived or typical flares are live, and it labels each one.

Reliability: NASA’s shared demo key was rate-limited when we tested it. The game falls back to archived flares, and a personal NASA key can be added with ?nasakey=.

Age fit: short pop-ups, one consistent box size, big readable text, and slow, gentle animations instead of shaking.

Accessibility: keyboard control, including the pause menu.

Accuracy: NASA photos are credited, and a few things are labelled as game imagination, such as the glowing crystals.

Judging: a quick Judge demo mode that jumps to a flare with the rover already built.

Limits: the team doesn’t code, so everything was built with AI help and checked by testing.
